historical_timeline.summary: Her mother dies eleven days after the birth.
A painful skin disease of one arm at about fourteen.
Her first child, born prematurely, dies after a few days.
Her daughter Clara and her son William die in Italy.
Her son Percy Florence is born.
Her husband drowns in the Gulf of Spezia.
Novels, a revised Frankenstein, and travel writing.
Recurrent headaches with transient right-sided paralysis and seizures begin.
Writes in her journal of ill health and extreme depression.
Lives at 24 Chester Square; her son marries in 1848.
Worsening illness with impaired speech and loss of power in one side.
Dies at Chester Square; the certificate records a supposed tumour of the left hemisphere.

claims.statement: Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin was born in London on August 30, 1797, the only child of the writer Mary Wollstonecraft and the philosopher William Godwin.

source_links.locator: Labour on Wednesday, the thirtieth of August

claims.statement: Her mother died in London on September 10, 1797, eleven days after the birth, of puerperal fever; her father wrote that the placenta had been retained and had to be removed by hand.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The Bodleian timeline and a reference biography say ten days; the dates in her father's memoir (birth August 30, death September 10) give eleven.

claims.statement: Her first child, a daughter born prematurely in February 1815, died after a few days.
claims.clinical_interpretation: No health facts about the child are used in this record.

claims.statement: She began the tale that became Frankenstein in Switzerland in the summer of 1816, and Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus was published anonymously in January 1818, when she was 20.
Her daughter Clara died in Italy in 1818, at about one year, and her son William died in Italy in June 1819, at three; she then had no living children.
claims.clinical_interpretation: No health facts about the children are used in this record.

claims.statement: Her son Percy Florence, born in November 1819, was the only one of her four children to survive childhood.
In June 1822 she nearly died of hemorrhage after a miscarriage about three months into a pregnancy; her husband stopped the bleeding by placing her in ice baths.

In July 1822 her husband, the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, drowned while sailing in the Gulf of Spezia, leaving her a widow before she was 25, with a son of two; she decided to earn her living by her writing and by publishing his.
She published the novels Valperga (1823) and The Last Man (1826), a revised Frankenstein (1831), and Rambles in Germany and Italy (1844).

At about fourteen she had a very painful skin condition of one entire arm, treated with poultices; at times she could not move the arm and wore it in a sling. It has been interpreted as eczema, psoriasis, or chickenpox.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her biographer Fiona Sampson as quoted in a 2022 paper; the diagnosis is uncertain.

claims.statement: In her journal in June 1840 she wrote that she had been long oppressed by care, disappointment, and ill health, and that lately ill health and extreme depression had marred what little she could do for others.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her own words; no diagnosis was made in her lifetime.

claims.statement: From 1839 she had recurrent severe headaches of varying severity, site, and duration, with dizziness, pain in the legs, right hand, and right eye, brief episodes of partial paralysis of the right leg and hand, tremors, and convulsive seizures. Her physicians called the illness psychosomatic in 1842, a functional derangement of the nerves or brain in 1845, and neuralgia of the heart in 1846.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her documented symptoms as summarized in a 2018 Lancet Neurology letter; the diagnoses are those of her time.

source_links.locator: Unilateral weakness, intermittent aphasia, and convulsive seizures over 12 years

claims.statement: From 1846 to 1851 she lived at 24 Chester Square, Belgravia, London, and spent time at Field Place in Sussex, the home of her son and his wife after their marriage in 1848.
claims.clinical_interpretation: An 1890 biography says the Chester Square house was given up in 1848 for one in Warwick Square; the 1889 biography and the blue plaque place her at Chester Square until her death.

claims.statement: Her symptoms worsened from late 1849, with impaired speech and difficulty moving; her nervous ailments increased until she lost power in one side, and she could not be moved from her house in Chester Square.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Later than the synthetic index visit; linked only to a later timeline event.

claims.statement: She died at Chester Square, London, on February 1, 1851, aged 53. Her death certificate recorded "Disease of the Brain Supposed Tumour in left hemisphere, of long standing." No autopsy was done.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The certificate's wording is documented; the tumour was supposed, not proven (see CLM-0016 and CLM-0017). The 1889 and 1890 biographies give February 21.

claims.statement: Her death has long been attributed to a brain tumour: the Bodleian Libraries describe a long illness possibly caused by a brain tumour, and a reference biography says she succumbed to one.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective interpretation resting on the death certificate's supposed tumour; no tissue or imaging exists.

claims.statement: A 2018 Lancet Neurology letter and a 2022 paper argue instead that twelve years of recurrent episodes make a tumour unlikely and that she had hemiplegic migraine with recurrent and finally fatal stroke; the 2022 paper links these to the skin disease of her adolescence.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluate headaches with transient numbness and weakness of one side in a 51-year-old writer: distinguish focal seizures from transient ischemic attack and migraine aura, obtain MRI with gadolinium and an EEG, and give driving and seizure-safety advice at once. Confirm a left convexity meningioma over the motor cortex with vasogenic edema and focal epilepsy; start levetiracetam and monitor mood and irritability; use dexamethasone only for symptomatic edema and briefly; present observation, resection, and stereotactic radiosurgery by shared decision-making (EANO 2021 and NCCN); grade the tumor by the WHO CNS5 criteria after resection, decide on adjuvant treatment by grade and extent of resection, and set the surveillance MRI schedule. Throughout, take a grief history and screen for depression in a woman with many early losses, and protect her ability to write. The teaching note contrasts this with the supposed tumour of the left hemisphere on her death certificate and the hemiplegic migraine hypothesis.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Shelley returns two weeks after presenting with headaches and spells of numbness and weakness of the right hand and leg. The MRI eleven days ago shows a 3.1 cm dural-based mass on the left frontoparietal convexity, over the part of the motor cortex that controls the right hand, with a dural tail and moderate swelling of the surrounding brain; its appearance is typical of a meningioma, and there is no stroke. The EEG a week ago shows sharp waves and slowing over the left central region. She had one more spell five days ago: tingling that climbed from her right fingers to the elbow, with twitching of the thumb, for about a minute, fully aware throughout. She has stopped driving. She saw Dr. Ferreira-Lindgren of neurosurgery this morning, looked at the images with him, and asked many questions. She was relieved that the spells have a cause that can be seen, and frightened by the word tumor. She has had no fall, confusion, or vomiting, and the morning headaches are unchanged.

assessment_plan.display: Left frontoparietal convexity meningioma with vasogenic edema
assessment_plan.assessment: A symptomatic meningioma with edema, causing seizures and mild right-hand weakness; the presenting concern is resolved into this diagnosis and focal epilepsy. Observation is not advised for a symptomatic tumor with edema. Stereotactic radiosurgery is less suitable for a 3.1 cm tumor with edema next to the motor cortex, and gives no tissue diagnosis. Resection aiming at removal of the tumor with its dural attachment (Simpson grade I) is likely to be curative and to relieve the seizures and weakness. She chose resection after hearing the three options with their benefits and risks
plan: Left craniotomy and resection in three weeks with Dr. Ferreira-Lindgren, with neuronavigation and motor mapping
Dexamethasone 4 mg twice a day from three days before surgery, then tapered after it; not started now, because the weakness is mild
MRI within 48 hours after surgery; pathology with WHO CNS5 grading

assessment_plan.display: Focal epilepsy due to the meningioma
assessment_plan.assessment: Recurrent focal aware seizures with a structural cause and an epileptiform EEG meet the definition of epilepsy, with a high risk of recurrence, so an antiseizure medicine is indicated now rather than prophylaxis
plan: Levetiracetam 500 mg twice a day from today; it can cause irritability or low mood, so tell the clinic if either appears
Keep a seizure diary; no driving until seizures are controlled for the period her state requires and the neurosurgeon agrees

hpi.narrative: Ms. Shelley returns three weeks after a left frontoparietal craniotomy. The tumor was removed completely with its dural attachment and a margin of dura (Simpson grade I), and the MRI the next day showed no residual tumor. The pathology is a meningothelial meningioma, CNS WHO grade 1: one mitosis per ten high-power fields, no brain invasion, no atypical features, Ki-67 3 percent, and no TERT promoter mutation or CDKN2A/B deletion. Her right hand was weaker for the first two days after surgery and has been improving steadily. She took dexamethasone for three days before surgery and stopped the taper eleven days ago. She has had no seizure since starting levetiracetam six weeks ago. She notices that she is short-tempered and tearful at times, which she links to the tablets as much as to the operation, and she has seen the counselor twice. The wound has healed and the staples are out. She has begun to write for half an hour a day.

assessment.display: Left frontoparietal convexity meningioma with vasogenic edema
assessment.assessment: The appearance is typical of a meningioma. Because it causes seizures and weakness and is surrounded by edema, observation is not appropriate. Stereotactic radiosurgery works best for small tumors without mass effect; at 3.1 cm with edema next to the motor cortex it carries a real risk of worsening the swelling, and it gives no tissue for grading. Surgical resection with its dural attachment (Simpson grade I) is the treatment of choice, is likely to be curative, and should relieve the seizures. The main risk is weakness of the right hand, usually temporary, which motor mapping during surgery reduces. She chose resection

assessment.display: Focal epilepsy due to the meningioma
assessment.assessment: Recurrent focal aware seizures with a causative lesion and an epileptiform EEG: an antiseizure medicine is indicated now. Levetiracetam suits her, with few interactions; its main drawback is irritability or low mood, which should be watched given her history

The deficit is mild and stable, so dexamethasone is not needed now. A short course from three days before surgery, tapered over about ten days afterwards, reduces brain swelling around the operation; longer use brings more harm than benefit

Grade decides adjuvant treatment. After complete resection of a CNS WHO grade 1 meningioma, radiation is not needed and follow-up is by MRI; grade 2 or 3 features (mitotic count, brain invasion, TERT promoter mutation, or CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion) would lead to a discussion of radiation

She should not drive until she has been seizure-free for the period her state requires and I have reviewed her after surgery. Writing can resume as soon as she feels able; occupational therapy helps if the hand is slow to recover
